title: A.4 Rigid Body Mechanics
subject: IBDP Physics
introduction: Rigid body mechanics studies the motion and equilibrium of objects that maintain their shape when forces act on them. Unlike particles, rigid bodies can rotate as well as translate. This topic explains concepts such as torque, angular motion, centre of mass and rotational equilibrium. These ideas are important in engineering, machines, structures and spacecraft.

definitions.meaning: An object that does not change shape when forces act on it.
The turning effect of a force around a pivot point.
The product of a force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
The point where the entire mass of an object can be considered to act.
The rate of change of angular displacement with time.
The rate of change of angular velocity with time.

core_concepts.heading: Rotational Motion
core_concepts.explanation: Rotational motion occurs when an object turns around an axis. Every point on the object moves in a circular path around the axis.

core_concepts.heading: Torque
core_concepts.explanation: Torque depends on the size of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot. A larger distance creates a larger turning effect.

core_concepts.heading: Rotational Equilibrium
core_concepts.explanation: An object is in rotational equilibrium when the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment.

core_concepts.heading: Centre of Mass
core_concepts.explanation: The centre of mass is the balance point of an object. The motion of an object can be analysed by considering all mass concentrated at this point.

formulas.name: Torque
formulas.explanation: Torque is the turning effect produced by a force. The turning effect increases when the force increases or when the distance from the pivot increases.

formulas.name: Angular Velocity
formulas.explanation: Angular velocity describes how quickly an object rotates.

formulas.name: Angular Acceleration
formulas.explanation: Angular acceleration describes the rate of change of angular velocity.

formulas.name: Rotational Equilibrium
formulas.explanation: For an object to remain balanced, the total turning effects in opposite directions must be equal.

formulas.name: Rotational Kinetic Energy
formulas.explanation: Rotating objects store kinetic energy depending on their rotational speed and distribution of mass.

moments_and_equilibrium.explanation: The principle of moments states that when an object is in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
steps: Draw all forces acting on the object.
Set clockwise moments equal to anticlockwise moments.

moments_and_equilibrium.explanation: The centre of mass is the point where the mass of an object can be considered concentrated. If the centre of mass lies above the support area, the object remains stable.

worked_examples.question: A force of 20 N acts at a distance of 3 m from a pivot. Calculate the torque.
A 50 N force acts 2 m clockwise from a pivot. Another force acts 5 m anticlockwise from the pivot. Find the second force for equilibrium.

rotational_dynamics.explanation: Moment of inertia is the rotational equivalent of mass. It describes how difficult it is to change the rotational motion of an object. It depends on the total mass and how far the mass is distributed from the axis of rotation.
The rotational version of Newton's second law connects torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
Angular momentum describes the amount of rotational motion an object has. It depends on moment of inertia and angular velocity.

angular_momentum_conservation.explanation: When no external torque acts on a system, angular momentum remains constant. A change in the distribution of mass changes rotational speed.
examples: A figure skater spins faster when pulling arms closer to the body.
Rotating spacecraft use conservation of angular momentum for attitude control.

engineering_applications.explanation: Aircraft designers analyse rotational motion to understand stability, control surfaces and turning behaviour.
Engineers use torque and rotational dynamics when designing motors, gears and machines.
Athletes use principles of centre of mass and angular momentum to improve performance.
Satellites use rotational mechanics to control orientation and maintain stability.

common_mistakes: Using distance instead of perpendicular distance when calculating moments.
Forgetting that torque is a vector quantity.
Confusing angular velocity with linear velocity.
Ignoring the position of the centre of mass.
Using mass instead of moment of inertia in rotational equations.
Forgetting that equilibrium requires both force and moment balance.
ib_exam_tips: Always identify the pivot before calculating moments.
Draw a clear diagram showing forces and distances.
Use perpendicular distance in torque calculations.
State clockwise and anticlockwise directions clearly.
Explain rotational principles using correct physics vocabulary.
Include units such as N m, rad/s and kg m².

hl_extension.explanation: Rolling objects combine translational and rotational motion. The total kinetic energy includes both movement of the centre of mass and rotation.
Rotating objects resist changes to their axis of rotation due to angular momentum.
Energy can transfer between rotational and translational forms depending on the system.

practice_questions.question: A 10 N force acts 4 m from a pivot. Calculate the torque.
Explain why a wide base increases stability.
practice_questions.answer: A wider base makes it harder for the centre of mass to move outside the support area.

practice_questions.question: Explain why a spinning skater rotates faster when their arms move closer to their body.
practice_questions.answer: Reducing the moment of inertia increases angular velocity while angular momentum remains conserved.

summary: Rigid body mechanics explains how objects rotate, balance and respond to turning forces. Understanding torque, moments, centre of mass and angular momentum allows physicists and engineers to analyse complex systems from machines to spacecraft.
